clue.text: Prometheus — and fine cast in film

indicators.note: to cast is to throw or mould into a new shape, so the letters of the two words are reshaped

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Reads like a review of a film about the Titan Prometheus, praising its fine cast.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cast' looks like the film's actors but signals the anagram; 'and' joins the two fodder words.
explanation.definitionFit: Spielberg's 1987 war drama, so it is an example of a film.

clue.text: Insect could be market leader, essentially

parts.note: something that could be may be so, written as one word

indicators.note: the essence sits at the heart of the phrase market leader, so its central four letters are taken

explanation.surface: Suggests some bug might become the top firm in its market.
explanation.walkthrough: 'essentially' takes the central letters of the two words run together as one, ETLE.
explanation.definitionFit: The cockchafer, a large brown beetle seen in late spring, is the insect of this name.

clue.text: Bone to pick with sons and daughters?

definitions.meaning: offspring, in the legal sense of a person's descendants

explanation.surface: Someone has a grievance to raise with their children.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means both a disputed matter and, formally, a person's offspring.

clue.text: Being in river, is fish no closer?

indicators.note: the river word is opened up and the other pieces placed in it

parts.note: the Exe is a river in Devon
taken as written

indicators.note: a closer is what ends something, so the fish word loses its final letter

parts.note: the tench is a freshwater fish

explanation.surface: Asks whether a fish in a river is getting any nearer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'no closer' cuts the fish's final letter; the Exe is a river in Devon, England.
explanation.definitionFit: Being as a noun means the state of living or being real, a synonym.

clue.text: Song and dance about ultimate in coffee blends

indicators.note: the fuss word goes around the letter picked from coffee

parts.note: making a song and dance is making a fuss

indicators.note: ultimate means last, so the final letter of coffee is taken

explanation.surface: Someone makes a big scene over the last of the coffee blends.
explanation.definitionFit: To fuse is to melt together or combine, so the verb is a synonym of blends.

clue.text: Greeting Little Nell primarily in annual celebration

parts.note: hallo is a variant of hello
wee is Scottish for small

indicators.note: primarily means first of all, so the opening letter of Nell is used

explanation.surface: Little Nell, the Dickens heroine, is greeted as part of some yearly festivity.
explanation.walkthrough: Little Nell is the heroine of Dickens's The Old Curiosity Shop; here 'Little' is split off for WEE.
explanation.definitionFit: The eve of All Saints' Day on 31 October is held every year, so an example of an annual festivity.

clue.text: Children holding tail of draught horse

indicators.note: the children word contains the picked letter

parts.note: seed in the biblical sense means offspring

indicators.note: the tail is the end, so the last letter of draught

explanation.surface: Kids hang onto the tail of a heavy carthorse.
explanation.walkthrough: 'draught horse' reads as one phrase, but draught only gives its last letter T and horse is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A steed is a horse, especially one ridden, a literary synonym.

clue.text: Writer's block — and poet is worried

indicators.note: worried letters are troubled and disturbed, so and poet is rearranged

explanation.surface: A poet anxious about writer's block, the inability to write.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Writer's block' looks like the creative condition but is read literally as a block of paper for writing on.
explanation.definitionFit: A pad of paper sheets, literally a block a writer uses, punning on the creative paralysis.

clue.text: Marbles provided by a wealthy American philanthropist

parts.note: Bill Gates, the Microsoft founder known for his foundation's giving

explanation.surface: A rich American benefactor supplies some marbles.
explanation.definitionFit: Agate is a banded stone and glass marbles are traditionally called by that name, so they are an example.

clue.text: Spanish paintings possibly brought back by George Orwell initially

indicators.note: initially takes the first letter of each of the two name words
brought back means the word is turned round to read backwards

parts.note: say, as in 'for example', means possibly

explanation.surface: Imagines Orwell, back from Spain, returning with some Spanish art.
explanation.walkthrough: Orwell fought in the Spanish Civil War, which feeds the surface. 'brought back' turns SAY into YAS.
explanation.definitionFit: Works by Francisco Goya, the Spanish painter, are called by his name in the plural.

clue.text: Very little admitted by audacious bankrupt

indicators.note: the audacious word lets the letter in, containing it

parts.note: insolent means cheekily bold, impudent
v is the small abbreviation for very

explanation.surface: A daring bankrupt confesses to having almost nothing.
explanation.definitionFit: Unable to pay one's debts; the two words are synonyms describing a failed debtor.

clue.text: That clothing before or after that

indicators.note: clothing means dressing or covering, so the word that wraps round the other piece

parts.note: taken as written
ere is an old word meaning before

explanation.surface: Reads like a fussy question about whether a garment comes first or later.
explanation.definitionFit: An archaic adverb meaning thereupon or on account of that, an old synonym.

clue.text: Rose made to wait in vain

definitions.meaning: jilted by a date who never turned up

explanation.surface: Someone named Rose was left waiting by a no-show date.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrasal verb means both got upright and failed to keep a date with someone.

clue.text: South African leaders can provide material

indicators.note: leaders are the first letters of the two words

parts.note: a tin is a can

explanation.surface: Politicians in South Africa can supply cloth.
explanation.definitionFit: A glossy woven fabric, so an example of material.

clue.text: Looking back, vagrant lost again

indicators.note: vagrant means wandering, so the letters stray into a new order

explanation.surface: A tramp lost his way again and keeps looking back.
explanation.walkthrough: 'vagrant' looks like a tramp but is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: A wistful yearning for the past is a looking back, used as a noun phrase.

clue.text: Tender marshal is unarmed

indicators.note: to marshal is to arrange in order, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A soft-hearted military officer goes about without weapons.
explanation.walkthrough: 'marshal' looks like an officer but is a verb signalling the anagram, and 'Tender' is a noun, one who tends.
explanation.definitionFit: A woman employed to look after children is one who tends them, so a tender.

clue.text: Scoundrel heading for distant American port

parts.note: a rotter is a cad or scoundrel

indicators.note: the head is the front, so the first letter of distant

explanation.surface: A villain makes for some far-off American harbour.
explanation.definitionFit: The Dutch city is Europe's largest seaport, so an example of a port.

clue.text: Nothing by a stream to shelter wild animal

indicators.note: by means next to, so the zero goes alongside the rest
the stream word houses the wild word inside it

parts.note: a rill is a small stream
mad means wild, crazy
O is nought, zero

explanation.surface: Something beside a brook protects a wild creature.
explanation.definitionFit: The armoured South American mammal is an example of an animal.

clue.text: Doctor proves hospital department was extravagant

indicators.note: to doctor is to tamper with or alter, so proves is rearranged

parts.note: ENT is ear, nose and throat, a hospital department

explanation.surface: A doctor shows that a hospital ward spent too much.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Doctor' is a verb here, rearranging PROVES into OVERSP.
explanation.definitionFit: Spending beyond one's means is being extravagant, past tense to match.

clue.text: Not knowing what is happening about old clothes

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so the clothes word goes round the other letter

parts.note: an outfit is a set of clothes

explanation.surface: Someone bewildered about dated garments.
explanation.definitionFit: The informal phrase means confused, unaware, dazed, an idiom.

clue.text: House martin finally going round French city

indicators.note: going round means turning about, so the combined letters read backwards

parts.note: a semi is a semi-detached house

indicators.note: finally takes the last letter of martin

explanation.surface: A bird nesting on a house circles a city in France.
explanation.walkthrough: 'House martin' looks like the bird, but House gives SEMI (a British semi-detached house) and martin just N.
explanation.definitionFit: A city in southern France known for its Roman arena, so an example of a French city.

clue.text: More blue snakes bottom up

indicators.note: the bottom letter of this down entry is moved up to the top

parts.note: adders are snakes, vipers

explanation.surface: Snakes turned belly up make someone more depressed.
explanation.definitionFit: Blue means sad, so more blue is the comparative synonym.

clue.text: Brown keeps high post for tall ship's constituent

indicators.note: keeps means holds, so the toast word contains the other piece

parts.note: to toast is to brown, as bread
PM, Prime Minister, is a high post in government

explanation.surface: Reads as if Gordon Brown, a former PM, holds a lofty job.
explanation.walkthrough: Brown looks like the former British Prime Minister Gordon Brown, but is the verb meaning toast.
explanation.definitionFit: The mast above the lower mast on a sailing vessel is part of a tall ship.

clue.text: Endless drink for law enforcement group

indicators.note: endless means without its end, so the final letter is dropped

parts.note: a posset is a hot drink of milk curdled with wine or ale

explanation.surface: Bottomless drinks for a squad of police officers.
explanation.definitionFit: A band summoned by a sheriff to enforce the law, a definition by description.

clue.text: Short treatise followed in recital

indicators.note: a recital is spoken out, so the word is taken by its sound

parts.note: tracked means followed, trailed

explanation.surface: A brief essay that was then performed at a recital.
explanation.definitionFit: A pamphlet or short essay, especially religious or political, a synonym of treatise.

clue.text: Corrected crossword setter turned over

indicators.note: turned means flipped round, so the setter word reads backwards

parts.note: the setter refers to themself as me
over means finished, ended

explanation.surface: A setter fixed a crossword by flipping it over.
explanation.walkthrough: 'turned over' reads as one phrase but splits in two: 'turned' reverses the setter, and 'over' means finished.
explanation.definitionFit: Emended means having had errors removed from a text, a synonym.

clue.text: First of youngsters in country, raised in nest

indicators.note: the letter goes inside the country word
raised in a down entry means written upwards, so the word reverses

parts.note: Eire is the Irish name for Ireland

indicators.note: first of takes the opening letter of youngsters

explanation.surface: Chicks raised in the countryside in a nest.
explanation.walkthrough: 'raised' turns EIRE into ERIE before the Y goes in.
explanation.definitionFit: The lofty nest of an eagle or other bird of prey, so a kind of nest.

clue.text: Perhaps sole protector for Welsh town

parts.note: the sole is one example of a fish, as 'perhaps' signals
a guard protects

explanation.surface: Maybe the only guardian of a town in Wales.
explanation.walkthrough: Fishguard is a port town in Pembrokeshire, west Wales.
explanation.definitionFit: A port town in Pembrokeshire with ferries to Ireland, an example of a Welsh town.

clue.text: Poet put out about weekend

indicators.note: about means around, so the annoy word encloses the letter

parts.note: to rile someone is to annoy them, put them out
the end of week is its last letter, k

explanation.surface: A poet upset about how his weekend went.
explanation.definitionFit: Rainer Maria Rilke was the Austrian-Bohemian lyric poet, so an example.

clue.text: Film's false teeth — premolars?

indicators.note: false means not genuine, so the letters are faked into a new order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Asks whether a film is about dentures replacing premolars.
explanation.walkthrough: 'false teeth' reads as dentures, but 'false' is the anagram signal for teeth and premolars together.
explanation.definitionFit: Bertolucci's 1987 biopic of Puyi, China's final emperor, so an example of a film.
